questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] the offline delivery leg for a team chat: mobile push notifications and unread badges layered onto the existing real-time hub (netslack, docs/architecture.md). Scenario: after an acquisition the workspace grows to 25,000 users; at any moment about 60% of them have no app open; the push provider accepts roughly 600 notifications a second for your account; product wants a phone badge that matches what the user would see in the app, and a 09:00 local-time digest of what each person missed overnight. Write your design before you look: who should be notified for a channel message and how the code decides membership today, how the system knows someone is offline, how a burst of messages becomes a sane number of pushes, where the badge number comes from, how the digest is scheduled and kept from sending twice, and how the push work is fed from the write path without being lost. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Start with the recipient list, because the table does not mean what it sounds like: a channel_members row is written when someone creates a channel or posts in a public one, and there is no endpoint to join without posting. A reader who never posted is not a member, so notifications need an explicit follow plus a per-member level (everything, mentions only, muted).

[w3] Feed the offline leg durably from the write: the domain already raises a MessagePosted event naming the message, channel, author and time, but the persistence mapping ignores domain events and nothing dispatches them. Store a notification intent in the same save as the message (an outbox) so a crash after the commit cannot drop the push work, and let a worker drain it.

[w3] The code has no notion of presence: the web client opens a hub connection only for the channel on screen and the hub records nothing when connections come and go. Offline has to be built as per-user presence in a shared store, a count of live connections with a grace period of a minute or two, and a user who is online but looking at another channel still needs the badge and maybe a desktop alert.

[w3] Coalesce per recipient and channel: the first message after a quiet period may notify at once, later ones within a window update one collapsible notification keyed by channel ('14 new in #incidents'), and mentions and direct messages skip the batching. With 15,000 offline followers and a 600-per-second ceiling, a single message already needs about 25 seconds of provider capacity, so one push per message per person cannot work.

[w3] The badge is a number the server owns: keep a last-read marker on each (channel, user) row, compute unread from it, put the server's current total in every push so the phone overwrites its badge instead of adding one, and have the app fetch the totals whenever it starts.

[w2] The digest needs data the profile lacks: a user holds a display name, email and avatar only, with no time zone, no device tokens and no notification settings. Add them, run the digest hourly for the users whose local clock reads 09:00, and record each (user, local date) sent so a re-run of the job skips them.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the push leg has run for a month. During an outage an incident channel takes 2,000 messages in 10 minutes and the push queue grows faster than the provider will accept; a message is deleted seconds after it was posted, yet its notification still lands on phones; a user reinstalls the app and the badge drifts away from what the app shows; and desktop users complain that their phones buzz while they are reading the chat. For each, what went wrong, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Per-message jobs explode: 2,000 messages times 15,000 offline followers is 30 million candidate notifications against about 360,000 the provider takes in those 10 minutes. Queue per-user state, not per-message work: one pending entry per (user, channel) whose count is updated in place, so the backlog is bounded by people, not traffic. The event already carries the ids that need.

[w3] When the queue outruns the ceiling, shed and prioritise rather than queue forever: a token bucket at the provider's rate, mentions and direct messages first, and a check at send time that drops a notification whose channel the user has read since it was queued, or that is older than a few minutes.
[w2] Make the backlog visible before users notice: alert on the age of the oldest queued notification and on provider rejections, not just on queue length.
keyPoints.quote: Add structured logs, distributed traces, metrics, alerts, and SLO dashboards.

keyPoints.text: [w3] There is no deletion today: a message can only be posted (its Edit method has no route), so deleting is new work. It must emit its own event that cancels a still-queued notification and replaces a delivered one under the same collapse id; sending only ids and letting the app load text after an access check means a removed message renders as gone.

[w3] A badge kept by the phone (plus one per push) starts at zero after a reinstall and drifts every time a push is merged or dropped. Only a server total survives that: the app asks for it at launch, every push carries it, and the last-read marker only ever moves forward, so reading on the laptop clears the phone.

[w2] The buzzing desk: the client tears its hub connection down whenever the viewer switches channel, so presence judged by connections flaps on every click, and judging offline by 'not in this channel's group' marks a reader of another channel as away. Presence has to be per user across all instances, with a grace period before anyone counts as offline.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your offline-delivery choices against the alternatives: one notification per message versus collapsed or batched notifications, unread state computed on the server for each user versus kept by each client, badge numbers maintained as each message is written versus counted when someone asks, presence from connection events versus heartbeats with a time-to-live, and how much of a message a push may carry once the workspace belongs to an enterprise. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] One notification per message is the simplest pipeline and shows every line on the lock screen, but its volume scales with traffic times followers and hits the provider ceiling in any burst; collapsing bounds the volume and the noise at the cost of per-user state, a short delay and a less precise preview. Many teams split it: mentions and direct messages at once, channel chatter collapsed.

[w3] Server-side unread is one truth for every device and survives a reinstall, paid for with a write each time something is marked read and a query whenever totals are shown; client-side unread is free for the server but disagrees across devices and resets with the app.

[w3] Maintaining badge numbers on write turns each post into a write per follower, which in a 25,000-person channel during a 2,000-message burst is tens of millions of row updates; counting on read uses the existing channel-and-time ordering to count rows past the marker only when a badge is needed, and a short per-user cache of the total keeps that cheap. Writes stay flat; reads pay instead.

[w2] Connection events are instant but noisy: the client reconnects automatically and drops its connection whenever the channel changes, and an instance that dies never reports its disconnects. Heartbeats with a time-to-live in a shared store are slower to notice a departure but correct after crashes and across instances.

[w2] An acquired company arrives with compliance rules, and text placed in a push travels through a third-party provider and sits on lock screens beyond your retention and deletion controls; ids-and-count payloads keep message content inside your own systems, at the cost of a fetch when the user opens the app.
keyPoints.quote: Add retention policies, legal hold, export, DLP, and eDiscovery requirements before enterprise rollout.
